Grouped Statistical Evidence for AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Model differences, metric disagreement, uncertainty, and ranking stability across the controlled evaluation framework

controlled_50 Painting is the independent unit Three complete core models Bounded SDXL evidence No combined trust score

1. Executive findings

This report consolidates the validated statistical evidence for restoration quality, model differences, metric disagreement, uncertainty, ranking stability, and compute. Painting is the independent unit. Repeated cases, regions, seeds, mask variants, and metric rows are not treated as independent paintings.

Overall metric winner LaMa 10 of 11 anchor wins
Bootstrap winner frequency 100.0% 5,000 painting-cluster resamples
Core quality population 1,080 360 nonzero cases × 3 models
Uncertainty groups 165 Prompt-specific repeated-seed groups
  • LaMa is the strongest computational restoration model in this evaluation. It ranks first overall and wins 10 of the 11 separate quality anchors.
  • OpenCV Telea is the main deterministic alternative. It wins crop SSIM and ranks second overall, showing that a classical method can remain competitive for local structural continuity.
  • Stable Diffusion ranks third overall. Its generative capacity does not compensate for weaker reference fidelity across most pixel, perceptual, feature, texture, colour, seam, and structural anchors.
  • Metric disagreement is real and useful. Different metric families do not always order paintings or models identically, so no combined quality or trust score is used.
Conclusion. LaMa is the best-performing model under the approved computational framework. This is a direct model comparison conclusion, but it is not a conservation approval.
Limitation. The repository contains only controlled_50. Between-dataset comparison is not_applicable_single_dataset. The ten SDXL candidates remain a bounded descriptive subset.

2. What was evaluated?

Candidate selection was fixed without inspecting metric values. The report compares the same 410 eligible cases for OpenCV Telea, LaMa, and the primary generic-prompt Stable Diffusion candidate. Empty-mask zero controls are retained as integrity evidence but excluded from ordinary restoration-quality inference.

Population element Count Interpretation
Controlled paintings 50 Independent statistical units
Evaluated restoration cases 410 Canonical, size, robustness, and synthetic-degradation cases
Core candidates 1230 410 each for Telea, LaMa, and Stable Diffusion
Nonzero core candidates 1080 Restoration-quality population after zero-control exclusion
Canonical zero controls 150 Integrity population; not ordinary restoration-quality evidence
Bounded SDXL candidates 10 Descriptive only
Quality anchors 11 Kept separate across ten families
Repeated-seed uncertainty groups 165 130 canonical and 35 damage-size groups

Evaluation policy

  • Eleven quality anchors remain separate across pixel, perceptual, feature, spatial, texture, colour, seam, semantic, and structural evidence.
  • Painting is the independent unit; repeated cases and candidates are reduced before population-level testing.
  • Runtime is operational evidence and does not enter quality ranking.
  • SDXL is descriptive only because only ten predeclared candidates were completed.
  • No combined quality, efficiency, uncertainty, or trust score is retained.
Conclusion. The evaluation population is balanced for the three core models and broad enough for painting-level paired comparison.
Limitation. The focused damage-size, mask-robustness, and synthetic-degradation experiments contain five paintings. Their category labels cannot be treated as independent category effects.

3. Overall model differences

Family-balanced ranking gives each evidence family one equal contribution. It does not reward a family merely because that family contains more metric rows.

Model Family-balanced rank Overall rank
LaMa 1.1 1.0
OpenCV Telea 2.0 2.0
Stable Diffusion 2.9 3.0
Model Anchor wins
OpenCV Telea 1
LaMa 10
Stable Diffusion 0

30 of the 33 paired model contrasts remain significant after within-family Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Effect direction and size remain visible by anchor instead of being compressed into one score.

Conclusion. LaMa is better overall because its advantage is repeated across nearly every quality family, not because one large metric table dominates the ranking.
Limitation. These effects measure reference fidelity and internal consistency. They do not establish historical authenticity or the acceptability of an intervention.

4. Category and canonical-damage patterns

The balanced canonical population contains ten independent paintings in each of five broad content categories. Category inference is therefore supported here, while a general style effect is not.

model_id Painting category OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
abstraction_surrealism 1.0 10.0 0.0
architecture_structured 0.0 11.0 0.0
high_texture_brushwork 1.0 10.0 0.0
landscape_natural 1.0 10.0 0.0
portrait_figure 0.0 11.0 0.0

0 of 33 model-specific category tests remain significant after FDR correction. The strongest model by anchor-win credit is: abstraction surrealism: LaMa; architecture structured: LaMa; high texture brushwork: LaMa; landscape natural: LaMa; portrait figure: LaMa.

model_id Canonical damage type OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
loss_large 1.0 10.0 0.0
loss_small 1.0 10.0 0.0
mixed_damage 1.0 10.0 0.0
scratch_thin 3.0 8.0 0.0

33 of 33 repeated canonical-damage tests remain significant after FDR correction. Anchor-win leaders are: loss large: LaMa; loss small: LaMa; mixed damage: LaMa; scratch thin: LaMa.

Conclusion. Model performance changes with content and damage type, but LaMa remains the most consistently strong model across the separate evidence anchors.
Limitation. Category is supported only for the balanced canonical population. Incomplete metadata prevents a general independent style or period conclusion.

5. Damage-size sensitivity

Seven predeclared target sizes from 2% to 20% were evaluated for the same five paintings. The rank trajectory shows whether a model remains competitive as the missing area grows.

model_id Damage level OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
size_02pct 2.1 1.50 2.40
size_04pct 2.1 1.40 2.50
size_06pct 2.4 1.20 2.40
size_08pct 2.3 1.25 2.45
size_10pct 2.3 1.15 2.55
size_15pct 2.4 1.10 2.50
size_20pct 2.3 1.25 2.45
  • Model ranks are recomputed at every damage level rather than assuming one global ordering.
  • Damage-size uncertainty is available for 35 Stable Diffusion groups with four seeds each.
  • Increasing damaged area and increasing seed variability are related questions, but they are not the same quantity.
Conclusion. Damage size is a meaningful stress condition: a model that performs well on small gaps is not automatically equally reliable on large missing regions.
Limitation. The damage-size experiment contains five paintings and one painting per broad category. Its trajectories are painting-specific rather than independent category effects.

6. Mask morphology and seed robustness

Mask robustness evaluates controlled changes in mask placement and geometry while holding the intended damage level fixed. Each robustness group contains five variants.

Model Robustness groups Median group rank Best group rank Worst group rank
OpenCV Telea 15 2.20 1.1 2.7
LaMa 15 1.25 1.0 1.9
Stable Diffusion 15 2.65 2.0 3.0
  • Lower median variant rank indicates more consistent preference across mask variants.
  • Rank spread reveals sensitivity that an overall average can hide.
  • Mask seed and morphology are input perturbations, not stochastic model-output uncertainty.
Conclusion. A trustworthy evaluation must test whether conclusions survive reasonable changes in mask geometry; one convenient mask is not enough evidence.
Limitation. The robustness experiment has no repeated Stable Diffusion generation seeds. Artificial uncertainty values are therefore not assigned.

7. Synthetic degradation

Synthetic degradation extends the binary missing-region tests to dirt and dust, partial transparency, water stain, and combined water-stain-and-dirt cases. The inputs approximate computational stress conditions rather than measured conservation states.

model_id Degradation family OpenCV Telea LaMa Stable Diffusion
dirt_dust 1.597 1.423 2.980
partial_transparency 2.567 1.427 2.007
water_stain 2.353 1.513 2.133
water_stain_dirt 2.440 1.240 2.320
  • Lower family-balanced case rank indicates stronger performance across the separate quality families.
  • Severity is ordinal and should not be interpreted as a calibrated material-condition scale.
  • The bounded SDXL cases provide examples, not a full four-model comparison.
Conclusion. Model ordering depends on degradation family, so binary-mask performance alone is insufficient for a broad restoration claim.
Limitation. Procedural degradations are controlled computational effects. They do not reproduce every optical, chemical, or material property of real painting deterioration.

8. Metric-correlation structure

Correlations are computed after reducing repeated evidence to one value per painting and model. All metrics are converted to directional utility before comparison, so positive correlation means similar painting ordering.

Conclusion. Metric agreement is model-dependent. Similarity between two metrics for one restoration method does not prove that the same metrics are interchangeable for another method.
Limitation. Correlation measures association, not correctness. Strong agreement can occur when two metrics share the same blind spot.

9. Metric and region disagreement

The predeclared comparisons retain disagreements between classical, perceptual, feature, semantic, texture, colour, and seam evidence. Rank-reversal fractions show how often two evidence views order paintings differently.

Predeclared comparison Model Spearman correlation Rank-reversal fraction Agreement status
classical_vs_lpips Stable Diffusion -0.336 0.624 inverse_association
semantic_vs_pixel Stable Diffusion -0.285 0.606 inverse_association
feature_vs_colour Stable Diffusion -0.018 0.505 inverse_association
semantic_vs_pixel OpenCV Telea 0.045 0.478 weak_agreement
feature_vs_seam OpenCV Telea 0.154 0.452 weak_agreement
feature_vs_colour OpenCV Telea 0.147 0.447 weak_agreement
feature_vs_seam LaMa 0.187 0.437 weak_agreement
feature_vs_seam Stable Diffusion 0.232 0.425 weak_agreement
psnr_vs_ssim Stable Diffusion 0.289 0.402 weak_agreement
classical_vs_lpips OpenCV Telea 0.356 0.376 weak_agreement
feature_vs_colour LaMa 0.362 0.375 weak_agreement
semantic_vs_pixel LaMa 0.405 0.359 moderate_agreement
  • PSNR or MAE agreement with SSIM does not guarantee agreement with perceptual or semantic evidence.
  • CLIP and DINOv2 measure related but non-identical feature behaviour.
  • Feature similarity can remain high while colour drift, texture mismatch, or boundary seams remain visible.
  • Twenty-three supported one-anchor region substitutions were tested; unsupported region combinations were not fabricated.
Conclusion. Metric disagreement is diagnostic evidence. It identifies cases where a single-number evaluation would be misleading.
Limitation. No computational metric in this report is designated as conservation truth. Disagreement cannot be resolved by simply choosing whichever metric favours a preferred model.

10. Uncertainty and performance

Stable Diffusion uncertainty is estimated from four repeated seeds inside each prompt-specific group. The generic and scratch-aware prompt arms remain separate.

Prompt arm Associations Median Spearman rho FDR-significant Positive adversity associations Paintings Seed groups
p00_generic 40 0.367 24 32 50 80
p05_scratch_aware 40 0.368 24 36 50 50

48 of 80 canonical uncertainty–performance associations remain significant after FDR correction. A positive coefficient means that greater seed variability is associated with worse reference-performance adversity for the paired scalar measure.

Conclusion. Repeated-seed variability can identify unstable generative cases, but low variability only means that candidates resemble one another. It does not prove that they are good restorations.
Limitation. Uncertainty is an empirical seed-variability proxy, not calibrated confidence. Mask robustness and synthetic degradation lack repeated-seed populations and receive no artificial values.

11. Ranking stability and sensitivity

The baseline family-balanced model order is tested by omitting each painting, omitting each evidence family, substituting supported regions, and resampling paintings. Zero controls are evaluated separately using the only applicable structural-affinity anchor.

Sensitivity analysis Rows Scenarios Winner retained Maximum rank change Minimum Kendall tau
baseline_rank 3 1 1.0 0.0 1.0
bootstrap_winner_stability 3 1 1.0 0.0 1.0
leave_one_evidence_family_out 30 10 1.0 0.0 1.0
leave_one_painting_out 150 50 1.0 0.0 1.0
region_policy_sensitivity 69 6 1.0 0.0 1.0
zero_control_sensitivity 3 1 1.0 1.0 —
  • The baseline winner is retained in 100.0% of the estimable non-zero-control sensitivity records.
  • LaMa receives 100.0% winner frequency across 5,000 painting-cluster bootstrap samples.
  • The zero-control structural-affinity comparison produces a complete three-model tie. Kendall and Spearman agreement are undefined for that constant rank vector.
Conclusion. The overall advantage of LaMa is not driven by one painting, one evidence family, or one supported region choice.
Limitation. The zero-control result is an integrity result, not evidence that the three models perform equally on actual restoration.

12. Quality and compute

Runtime is reported because deployment cost matters, but it remains separate from quality. Quality–runtime associations are computed for every core model and every anchor without producing an efficiency score.

Model Candidates Median seconds Mean seconds Minimum seconds Maximum seconds
OpenCV Telea 410 0.424 0.453 0.251 1.020
LaMa 410 1.567 1.598 0.202 2.395
Stable Diffusion 410 9.533 8.439 0.249 10.217
SDXL 10 294.916 378.469 207.408 599.522
  • OpenCV Telea is the fastest method and provides a practical deterministic baseline.
  • LaMa combines stronger overall metric performance with higher compute cost than Telea.
  • Stable Diffusion and especially the bounded SDXL executions require substantially more generative compute.
Conclusion. The best quality model is not automatically the fastest model. Method selection should state whether speed or restoration fidelity has priority.
Limitation. Runtime depends on recorded hardware, software, batching, caching, and system load. These measurements are not universal benchmarks.

14. Supported conclusions and limitations

RQ1 — How should restoration quality be evaluated?

Quality must be evaluated with complementary pixel, perceptual, feature, texture, colour, seam, semantic, and structural evidence. Metric disagreements are findings, not noise to average away.

RQ2 — How do restoration methods compare?

LaMa is the strongest overall computational model, OpenCV Telea is the fast deterministic alternative, and Stable Diffusion is weaker on most reference-fidelity anchors despite generating plausible content.

RQ3 — Does uncertainty identify unreliable cases?

Repeated-seed variability provides useful instability evidence for the canonical and damage-size Stable Diffusion populations. It is not calibrated confidence and cannot establish correctness.

Supported conclusions

  • LaMa is the best core model under the approved computational evidence framework.
  • OpenCV Telea is faster and can remain competitive on local structural continuity.
  • Stable Diffusion requires explicit uncertainty and failure inspection; visual plausibility is insufficient.
  • Model ordering should be stress-tested across damage size, mask geometry, degradation family, metric family, and region.

Claims not supported

  • historical authenticity;
  • conservation suitability or treatment approval;
  • museum approval;
  • a general independent style effect;
  • a between-dataset comparison;
  • a full four-model SDXL comparison;
  • calibrated probabilistic confidence.
Conclusion. Trustworthiness comes from transparent evidence coverage, visible disagreement, sensitivity testing, and scoped claims—not from a universal trust score.
Limitation. All results remain computational evaluations on controlled images. Human conservator review and historically grounded assessment remain necessary for real restoration decisions.
